procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Madhya Pradesh.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 7, 1968, of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 519 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State appealed to the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The High Court accepted the prosecution's appeal in part, confirming convictions and sentences under sections 342 and 353 of the Indian Penal Code, but modifying the conviction under section 332 to a one-year rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (originally convicted) approached the Supreme Court by special leave, filing two appeals (Criminal Appeal Nos. 80 and 81 of 1969).

decision.appeal_result: The appeal except to the extent indicated is dismissed.
decision.conviction_status: The conviction under s. 332 is set aside and the convictions under sections 342 and 353 are confirmed.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence under s. 332 is set aside and the sentence under sections 342 and 353 is confirmed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the illegality of a search conducted under Section 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code justifies the commission of subsequent criminal acts like wrongful confinement (Section 342 IPC) and assault on a public servant (Section 353 IPC) against the investigating officer.

facts: An investigating officer (P.W. 1) conducted a search and seized currency notes from the appellants' office.
The appellants argued that this search was illegal because the officer did not record the reasons for it in writing, as required by Section 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
Following the search, the appellants forcibly brought the officer back into the office, threatened him, and would not allow him to leave until he provided a written statement.
The appellants were charged with wrongful confinement (Section 342 IPC) and assault on a public servant (Section 353 IPC) for these subsequent actions.
law: Section 165 of the Cr.P.C. requires an investigating officer to record in writing the grounds for their belief before conducting a search without a warrant.
The appellants contended that a failure to comply with Section 165 makes the entire investigation illegal, thereby justifying any obstruction during the subsequent process.
Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defines the offense of wrongful confinement, which is restraining a person in a way that prevents them from moving beyond certain limits.
Section 353 of the IPC pertains to assaulting or using criminal force against a public servant in the execution of their duty.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, calling it a "fallacy."
The Court drew a clear distinction between the act of the search itself and the criminal acts that occurred after the search was completed.

It reasoned that any non-compliance with Section 165 is confined to the legality of the "actual search and seizure." Once the search is complete, that provision no longer applies to subsequent steps in the investigation.

The Court stated that while obstructing an illegal search *as it is happening* might be justified, this does not give a person a "licence" to commit subsequent criminal acts like assault and wrongful confinement.
Specifically, the Court noted that the offense of wrongful confinement (Section 342 IPC) is a general offense that has "nothing to do with the investigation or search."
Therefore, the illegality of the initial search could not be used as a defense or justification for the appellants' later actions of forcibly detaining and assaulting the officer.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, holding that the illegality of a search under Section 165 Cr.P.C. does not justify the subsequent commission of separate criminal offenses like wrongful confinement and assault against the investigating officer. The justification for obstruction is limited to the illegal search itself and does not extend to acts committed after the search is complete.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 332 of the Indian Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duty was sustainable.

facts: The appellants argued that their conviction under Section 332 was unsustainable because they had not been formally charged with that specific offense, and this lack of charge prejudiced them.
The advocate for the respondent (the state/prosecution) did not insist on the conviction under Section 332 being upheld.
application: The Court noted that since it was already confirming the convictions and sentences of the appellants under two other sections (342 and 353), it was not necessary to examine the legality of the conviction under Section 332.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the conviction and sentence under Section 332 without going into the legal merits of the issue, based on the appellants' argument, the respondent's concession, and the confirmation of convictions on other charges.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the illegality of a search conducted under Section 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code justifies the commission of subsequent criminal acts like wrongful confinement (Section 342 IPC) and assault on a public servant (Section 353 IPC) against the investigating officer.
appellant_arguments: The appellants contended that their actions of wrongfully restraining, obstructing, and assaulting the investigating officer (P.W. 1) did not constitute an offence because they had a right to obstruct an illegal search.
They argued the search was illegal because the officer failed to record reasons as required by Section 165 of the Cr.P.C. and did not provide a list of seized items as per Section 103, Cr.P.C.
This illegality, they submitted, vitiated the entire investigation, and consequently, any obstruction during the investigation was not an offence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the non-observance of the provisions of Section 165, Cr.P.C. was a mere irregularity.
The investigating officer (P.W. 1) was acting in an honest and bona fide manner in the discharge of his duties.
Therefore, the appellants were not justified in claiming a right of private defence to obstruct and man-handle the officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 332 of the Indian Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt to deter a public servant from his duty was sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that they were entitled to an acquittal for the offence under Section 332 because they were not formally charged with it, and the conviction was therefore prejudicial to them.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's advocate did not insist on the conviction under Section 332 being upheld.

cases.case_name: The Stare of Rajasthan v. Rahman
cases.principle: An illegality in a search, such as the failure to record the grounds of belief before conducting it, does not render the entire investigation illegal or justify obstructing public servants from discharging their duties, because the power to conduct the search is derived from the statute itself, not from the procedural compliance.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The illegality of a search, due to non-compliance with procedural requirements, is confined to the act of the search and seizure itself. Such illegality does not provide a legal justification for committing separate criminal acts after the search and seizure is complete.
obiter: Obstruction during the course of a search that does not conform with procedural requirements might be justified.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While an obstruction during the course of a search not conducted in conformity with Section 165 Cr.P.C. might be justified, this does not provide a warrant for committing subsequent and separate criminal acts. The non-conformity with search provisions is confined to the actual search and seizure and does not taint the entire investigation or entitle a person to wrongfully confine or assault an officer after the search is complete, as such actions are not a defensive obstruction but an offensive compulsion.
legal_tests_applied: The court distinguished between a 'defensive act' of obstructing an ongoing illegal search and an 'offensive act' of compulsion, such as forcing an officer to return and perform acts against their will after the search has concluded.

The court applied a temporal and scope-based limitation on procedural illegalities, holding that the non-conformity with Section 165 Cr.P.C. is confined to the specific part of the investigation related to the search and seizure and does not extend to or invalidate subsequent steps in the investigation.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the illegality of the search continues during the whole process of investigation, stating, 'once the search and seizure is complete that provision ceases to have any application to the subsequent steps in the investigation.'

The court found that the appellants' actions went beyond mere obstruction, reasoning that 'where search has ended and the persons conducting the search have left the premises, to bring them back and to make them do things against their will is not an obstruction to an act but a compulsion to make them act.'
The court held that justification for obstruction during an illegal search does not 'entitle a person to force a public servant or any other person to do acts contrary to their volition.'

The court determined that the offence of wrongful confinement under Section 342 is a general offence that 'has nothing to do with the investigation or search' and therefore cannot be justified by an illegality in the search.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that even if the search was illegal, the officer was acting in a bona fide manner in the discharge of his duties, and the appellants were not justified in their subsequent actions.

The court found that the appellants' actions of forcibly taking the officer from the road, detaining him in the office, and threatening him constituted the distinct offence of wrongful confinement, separate from the preceding search.
The court noted that the officer was prevented from complying with the requirement to provide a list of seized items (Section 103 Cr.P.C.) by the appellants' own aggressive and abusive behavior.
policy_considerations: Accepting the proposition that an initial illegality in an investigation justifies subsequent obstruction would 'encourage people to take the law into their hands, frustrate the investigation of crimes and thwart public justice.'
The court stated that accepting the appellants' argument 'would be to confer a licence and afford them an unwarranted excuse to commit each and every criminal act.'
